title: The Job Hunt
description: Navigate the emotionally charged world of job searching after a layoff. From updating your resume to acing interviews and evaluating competing offers, every decision shapes your career trajectory.
theme: Navigating career transitions and job searching
learning_objectives: Develop resilience and self-worth when facing rejection
Practice strategic self-presentation in high-stakes situations
Understand how to leverage networks effectively and authentically
Build confidence in negotiating your value in the job market
Recognise when to be patient vs. when to take action in a job search
learning_concept: A job search is a marathon disguised as a sprint — the candidates who succeed combine strategic effort with emotional resilience and a clear sense of their own worth.
psychological_framework: Self-Determination Theory (Deci and Ryan) — autonomy, competence, and relatedness as drivers of motivation during career transitions

chapters.title: The Search
chapters.teaser: You have been laid off. The clock is ticking and your options are unclear...

chapters.title: The Interview
chapters.teaser: You've landed interviews — now you have to perform under pressure.

chapters.title: The Decision
chapters.teaser: Two very different offers on the table. The wrong choice could cost you years.

chapters.title: The First 90 Days
chapters.teaser: You got the job — but keeping it requires a whole new set of skills.

chapters.title: The Career You Choose
chapters.teaser: Six months in — the job is secure, but the bigger question remains: is this who you want to be?

glossary_terms.definition: The way you present your professional identity, skills, and values to employers and the industry.
A casual conversation with someone in a role or company you are interested in, used to gather insights rather than apply for a job.
Software used by employers to filter and rank resumes based on keywords before a human ever reads them.
A structured way of answering interview questions: Situation, Task, Action, Result.
A response to a job offer where you propose different terms, such as a higher salary or better benefits.
The process of integrating a new employee into an organisation, including training, introductions, and cultural orientation.
The persistent feeling that you do not deserve your success or position, despite evidence of your competence.
The ability to get things done and persuade others without having formal power or a management title over them.
A formal assessment of an employee's work quality, achievements, and areas for development, typically conducted periodically.
An alternative job or salary offer used to retain an employee who is considering leaving for another opportunity.

scenes.title: The Email No One Wants
scenes.narrative: On a Tuesday morning, you receive the email that changes everything: 'Due to organisational restructuring, your role at TechCorp has been eliminated, effective 30 days from today.' You stare at the screen in your Mumbai flat. Your EMI is due in three weeks. Your savings will cover four months at most. Your former colleague Arjun texts: 'Same here. They let 40 of us go.' The panic is real — but somewhere underneath it, you feel a flicker of something unexpected. Maybe this is the reset you needed.
scenes.image_prompt: A young Indian professional staring at a laptop screen showing a layoff email in a Mumbai apartment, mixed expression of shock and quiet resolve, morning light, photorealistic
scenes.coaching_moment: Involuntary transitions feel like failure but often contain the most important career turning points. Your first response sets the emotional tone for the entire search.
scenes.reflection_prompt: How do you respond when something you didn't choose forces you to reconsider your path?

choices.label: Take 48 hours to process before doing anything — emotional clarity first
choices.description: The rush to act from panic rarely produces good decisions.

choices.label: Update your LinkedIn and resume today — get ahead of the process immediately
choices.description: Action combats anxiety. Start the machine now.

choices.label: Call three former colleagues and mentors — understand the market before applying
choices.description: Warm contacts are 10x more valuable than cold applications.

scenes.title: The Spray-and-Pray vs. The Targeted Approach
scenes.narrative: Two weeks in. You have two strategies in front of you. Option one: apply to 30 jobs on Naukri and LinkedIn this week, casting a wide net and hoping for volume. Option two: identify 8 target companies, research them thoroughly, and send personalised applications. Your friend Shreya swears by the spray-and-pray method: 'It's a numbers game.' But your mentor Sunita disagrees: 'In this market, quality beats quantity every time.'
scenes.image_prompt: Young Indian professional at a desk with two approaches mapped out on paper, job listings on one screen, company research on another, decisive expression, home office setting, photorealistic
scenes.coaching_moment: In job searching, as in life, depth usually beats breadth. A well-targeted, researched application signals something generic applications never can — that you genuinely want this specific role.

choices.label: Go targeted — research 8 companies and write genuine personalised applications
choices.description: Slower. More effort. But each application stands out.

choices.label: Spray-and-pray — 30 applications by Friday keeps all options open
choices.description: Speed and volume. At least one should stick.

scenes.title: The Referral Ask
scenes.narrative: You spot a Senior Product Manager role at a company you've admired for years — Razorpay. The job posting went live this morning. You notice that Vikram, an old IIM classmate you haven't spoken to in two years, works there. You have two weeks before applications close. Asking Vikram for a referral feels uncomfortable — you lost touch after a group project dispute. But a referral could be the difference between the ATS bin and a real human reading your resume.
scenes.image_prompt: Young Indian professional looking at an old contact's LinkedIn profile with hesitation and determination, WhatsApp chat open, weighing a difficult ask, photorealistic
scenes.coaching_moment: Asking for help when we need it requires more courage than we often expect — but most people are more willing to help than we assume. The worst answer is no.

choices.label: Reach out to Vikram, acknowledge the gap, and ask directly for a referral
choices.description: Honest and direct. The project dispute is history.

choices.label: Apply directly without a referral — you don't want to owe anyone anything
choices.description: Self-reliance. But pride has a cost.

choices.label: Reconnect with Vikram without mentioning the job first — rebuild the relationship
choices.description: Long play — authentic reconnection before the ask.

scenes.title: The First Round
scenes.narrative: You have a first-round video call with Razorpay's hiring manager, Priya Sharma. Five minutes in, she asks the question every job-seeker dreads: 'I see you were laid off. Can you walk me through what happened and what you learned from it?' The question hangs in the air. You can feel the temptation to spin it, to make the layoff sound like it was actually your choice. But Priya has sharp eyes and you sense she has heard every version of that spin before.
scenes.image_prompt: Indian professional on a professional video call with a hiring manager, focused and composed, laptop with virtual background, professional home setting, photorealistic
scenes.coaching_moment: Authenticity in interviews is more compelling than polish. Hiring managers who ask hard questions are testing for self-awareness, not for perfection.

choices.label: Be completely honest — explain the layoff, own the learnings, show what changed
choices.description: Vulnerability with insight is rare and deeply impressive.

choices.label: Acknowledge the layoff briefly and pivot quickly to your achievements
choices.description: Professional redirect. Keep the narrative positive.

scenes.title: The Technical Round
scenes.narrative: You progress to the technical case study round. The prompt: 'Razorpay wants to expand into MSME lending. Design the first version of the product.' You have 45 minutes. Halfway through, you realise your initial framework is weak — you started with solutions instead of user problems. You can either continue with your current answer to stay within time, or restart with a better approach and risk running out of time.
scenes.image_prompt: Indian professional working on a case study on paper and laptop, halfway through, looking at what they have and what they wish they had done differently, focused tension, photorealistic
scenes.coaching_moment: The ability to recognise a wrong direction mid-execution and course-correct — even at personal cost — is the mark of a strong thinker. Perfect is the enemy of good only if good is actually good enough.
scenes.reflection_prompt: When you realise you are on the wrong path halfway through, do you push ahead or restart?

choices.label: Restart from user-first framework — even if you need 10 extra minutes
choices.description: Courage to change course. Quality over completion.

choices.label: Finish the current approach and add a note acknowledging the methodology gap
choices.description: Self-awareness within constraints — still shows you noticed.

scenes.title: The Final Round Curveball
scenes.narrative: The final round is a panel interview. At the end, the hiring director asks: 'We noticed you applied to three other companies this week. Why should we believe Razorpay is your first choice?' The question is a trap designed to test composure and honesty. You did apply elsewhere — that is simply responsible job searching. How you answer this will define whether they see you as desperate, deceptive, or strategically confident.
scenes.image_prompt: Indian professional in a formal panel interview facing multiple interviewers, composed under pressure, corporate meeting room, photorealistic
scenes.coaching_moment: Confidence under interrogation does not require deception — it requires clarity about your own value and the honesty to own your choices without apology.

choices.label: Be honest: 'I am exploring responsibly, but Razorpay is my top choice because...' and give specific reasons
choices.description: Honest and compelling. Shows strategy, not desperation.

choices.label: Say Razorpay is your only focus — bend the truth to protect the opportunity
choices.description: Risky. Experienced interviewers often sense dishonesty.

scenes.title: Two Offers, One Week
scenes.narrative: Against the odds, two offers arrive in the same week. Offer A: Razorpay, Senior PM, ₹28 LPA, exciting product, strong brand, demanding culture with known 70-hour work weeks. Offer B: A Series B startup, Head of Product, ₹22 LPA but meaningful equity, earlier stage, higher risk, potentially transformative if it works. You have until Friday to decide. Your parents want you to take the safe brand name. Your mentor wants you to take the equity bet.
scenes.image_prompt: Indian professional at a kitchen table with two offer letters side by side, thoughtful and weighing both options, partner or family member visible in background, warm evening light, photorealistic
scenes.coaching_moment: Career decisions are not just about money or title — they are about the life you are choosing to live for the next three to five years. Know what you actually value.
scenes.reflection_prompt: How much of what you value at work is about the work itself versus what others think of your choice?

choices.label: Take the Razorpay offer — the brand and learning environment are worth the trade-off
choices.description: Strong platform, strong resume-builder, known culture.

choices.label: Take the startup offer — the equity and ownership are worth the risk
choices.description: High-risk, high-reward. You will learn by doing everything.

scenes.title: The Negotiation
scenes.narrative: You have decided which offer to accept — but you haven't signed yet. A colleague who took a similar role last year tells you: 'Everyone negotiates. If you don't, you're leaving money on the table and signalling that you don't know your worth.' Your salary ask feels awkward. The number you want is 15% higher than their offer. You've never negotiated a salary before. Your mouth goes dry just thinking about it.
scenes.image_prompt: Indian professional on a phone call with an HR recruiter, notes prepared for negotiation, determined expression, pacing in a room, photorealistic
scenes.coaching_moment: Salary negotiation is not confrontation — it is a professional expectation. Employers make their best offer first only if they assume candidates will not push back.

choices.label: Negotiate confidently for 15% more, backed by market data
choices.description: Know your worth and ask for it directly.

choices.label: Accept the offer as-is — you are grateful and don't want to seem difficult
choices.description: Gratitude is good. Under-valuing yourself is costly.

choices.label: Negotiate for non-salary benefits — extra leave, remote flexibility, or a signing bonus
choices.description: Creative negotiation. Total compensation includes more than money.

scenes.title: Day One
scenes.narrative: You walk into your new office on a Monday morning. The nervousness is real but different from the fear of the layoff — this is the nervous energy of possibility. You think of the 63 applications, 4 rejections, 2 near-misses, and the months of uncertainty that brought you here. Your new manager shakes your hand and says: 'We are really glad you chose us.' And for the first time in months, you feel like yourself again.
scenes.image_prompt: Indian professional on their first day at a new job, walking through a modern office reception, ID badge in hand, confident and fresh, warm welcoming light, photorealistic
scenes.coaching_moment: Resilience is not the absence of fear during hard times — it is the ability to keep moving through uncertainty without losing your sense of who you are.

choices.label: 'The layoff was the best thing that happened to my career — it forced me to get clear'
choices.description: Post-traumatic growth. The hard path led somewhere real.

choices.label: 'I would do the search differently — more strategy, less anxiety'
choices.description: Growth through honest reflection. The next transition will be handled better.

scenes.title: The Onboarding Maze
scenes.narrative: Week two at your new job. The onboarding programme is chaotic — three different systems to learn, a 200-page product wiki that is outdated, and a manager who is travelling for two weeks. Your peers seem busy and unapproachable. The imposter syndrome hits hard: everyone else looks like they know what they are doing. You wonder if you are the only one who feels lost. Then you overhear a colleague in the break room saying: 'I faked it for three months before I understood anything here.'
scenes.image_prompt: Indian professional at a new workplace desk looking overwhelmed by onboarding materials, multiple screens and documents, colleagues busy around them, modern Indian office, photorealistic
scenes.coaching_moment: Everyone feels lost in the first weeks of a new job. The ones who succeed fastest are the ones who ask for help early instead of pretending they do not need it.

choices.label: Identify the most approachable team member and ask them to be an informal buddy for your first month
choices.description: Humble and strategic. One good guide is worth a hundred documents.

choices.label: Spend evenings and weekends studying the product wiki until you are fully up to speed
choices.description: Self-reliance through effort. Slow but thorough.

choices.label: Schedule 15-minute coffee chats with five team members to understand the team and product simultaneously
choices.description: Build relationships while learning. Two goals, one approach.

scenes.title: The First Conflict
scenes.narrative: In your third week, a senior colleague dismisses your suggestion in a team meeting with a curt: 'We tried that two years ago. It did not work.' The dismissal is public and feels personal. You are not sure if this is normal pushback or if you are being hazed as the new person. Later, another colleague messages you privately: 'Don't take it personally — Rahul does that to everyone. But your idea was actually good.' The question is not whether you were right — it is how you handle being publicly shot down.
scenes.image_prompt: Indian professional looking composed but stung after being publicly dismissed in a meeting, colleagues around a conference table, modern office, photorealistic
scenes.coaching_moment: How you respond to your first public setback in a new job signals to the entire team who you are. Reacting with ego or withdrawal both cost you — responding with composure and curiosity wins.

choices.label: Approach Rahul privately after the meeting and ask: 'Can you tell me what went wrong when you tried this before?'
choices.description: Curiosity over ego. Learn from his experience while earning his respect.

choices.label: Let it go and prove yourself through your work over the next month
choices.description: Actions speak louder than arguments. Earn credibility through delivery.

scenes.title: The First Win
scenes.narrative: Six weeks in, your manager returns from travel and assigns you a small but visible project: redesigning the client onboarding flow for a new market segment. You throw yourself into it — user interviews, competitor analysis, three iterations. When you present the final design to the product team, there is a moment of silence. Then your manager says: 'This is better than what we had before you joined.' Rahul nods. It is not applause — it is something better: professional respect earned through work.
scenes.image_prompt: Indian professional presenting a well-prepared design to a product team, colleagues looking impressed, manager nodding approvingly, modern meeting room, photorealistic
scenes.coaching_moment: Your first real contribution at a new job changes how the team sees you — from 'the new person' to 'someone who adds value.' That transition is earned, not given.

choices.label: Thank the team for the feedback and acknowledge what you learned from the colleagues who helped
choices.description: Grace in success. Credit those who supported you.

choices.label: Use this momentum to pitch a larger project that could have even bigger impact
choices.description: Strike while the credibility is fresh. Ambition after evidence.

scenes.title: The Performance Review
scenes.narrative: Your six-month performance review arrives. Your manager gives you a 'Strong Performer' rating — in the top 20% of the team. She mentions a possible promotion path in 12 months. But she also gives you constructive feedback: 'You are excellent at individual execution, but you need to develop your ability to influence without authority. The next level requires getting things done through other people.' The feedback is fair and uncomfortable at the same time.
scenes.image_prompt: Indian professional in a one-on-one performance review with a manager, both looking at a document, thoughtful and constructive atmosphere, private meeting room, photorealistic
scenes.coaching_moment: The most valuable feedback in your career is the kind that names the specific gap between where you are and where you want to be. Receive it as a gift, even when it stings.

choices.label: Ask your manager for a specific project where you can practice influencing across teams
choices.description: Turn feedback into action. Seek the stretch assignment.

choices.label: Find a mentor outside your direct team who is known for cross-functional leadership
choices.description: Learn from someone who has already mastered the skill you are building.

scenes.title: The Counter-Offer
scenes.narrative: A recruiter from a competitor calls with a compelling offer: 40% salary increase, a senior title, and equity. The role is interesting but the company has a reputation for high turnover and intense pressure. Your current company has invested in you, and you genuinely enjoy the team. But 40% is a life-changing salary difference. Arjun, your old colleague who was also laid off, messages: 'I jumped for money twice and regretted it both times. Think about the whole picture.'
scenes.image_prompt: Indian professional weighing a competing job offer while looking at photos and memories from current workplace, contemplative expression, evening setting, photorealistic
scenes.coaching_moment: Career decisions made purely on salary often trade long-term growth for short-term gain. Know the whole cost of what you are choosing — and what you are leaving.
scenes.reflection_prompt: When you look at your career five years from now, what matters more — the number on the paycheck or the person you became?

choices.label: Stay — the growth opportunity, team, and culture are worth more than the salary gap
choices.description: Long-term investment in yourself. Loyalty to a good situation.

choices.label: Use the competing offer to negotiate a raise at your current company — market data is leverage
choices.description: Strategic use of information. Know your worth and ask for it.

scenes.title: The Year-End Reflection
scenes.narrative: One year since the layoff email that changed everything. You sit at your desk — not the one in the Mumbai flat where panic set in, but the one you have earned, in a role that challenges you, with a team that respects you. You think about the 63 applications, the rejection emails, the interview where you chose honesty over spin, and the salary negotiation that made your hands shake. You are not the same person who received that email a year ago. You are someone who has been tested and chose to grow rather than shrink. That is the real career asset no company can give you or take away.
scenes.image_prompt: Indian professional at their desk at the one-year mark, looking out the window with quiet confidence, workspace personalised with small meaningful items, warm golden hour light, photorealistic
scenes.coaching_moment: A career is not a straight line — it is a series of recoveries, decisions, and small acts of courage. The person you become through the process is worth more than any title on a business card.

choices.label: 'The layoff was not a chapter I would have chosen — but it became the one that defined me most'
choices.description: Post-traumatic growth. The unwanted turning point became the necessary one.
choices.ending_message: One year ago you were laid off and terrified. Today you are a top performer in a role you earned through strategy, resilience, and the refusal to let fear make your decisions. The layoff did not define you — your response to it did. Every interview, every rejection, every negotiation made you someone who knows their worth and is not afraid to claim it. That is the career lesson no business school can teach.

choices.label: 'Next time, I will be prepared before the crisis hits — not after'
choices.description: The lesson that transforms the next transition from crisis to opportunity.
choices.ending_message: You survived the storm and you know exactly what you would do differently next time — maintain your network before you need it, keep your skills sharp before the market demands it, and never let a job title become your entire identity. The next career transition will find you ready, not reactive. That preparation is the most valuable asset you built this year.

coaching_moment: A job search is a marathon disguised as a sprint — the candidates who succeed combine strategic effort with emotional resilience and a clear sense of their own worth.
cultural_context: India's youth unemployment and skills mismatch are significant economic challenges. This game develops the self-awareness, persistence, and strategic thinking that help young Indians navigate an increasingly competitive job market.
reflection_prompt: Looking back at the choices you made, which one felt hardest and why? What would you do differently if you replayed?
